about: Packages and domains with published evidence. 'finding' is one of: confirmed_telemetry, advertising, malware_indicator, suspected_tracking, connected_service, unknown_traffic. Nothing is listed on a name match alone. 'category' is the debloater category this entry gets on any device; a device profile can only make it stricter.

packages.name: Adups FOTA (firmware updater)
packages.purpose: Over-the-air firmware updates on many low-cost MediaTek devices.
packages.evidence: Kryptowire (Nov 2016) found versions of this app sending the content of text messages, call logs, contacts and device identifiers to bigdata.adups.com. Adups later shipped versions without that collection; Malwarebytes reports newer versions do not contain the backdoor code.
packages.risk: It is also the firmware updater: with it disabled, the unit gets no OTA updates from the seller. Which version a head unit carries is not known until it is checked.
sources: https://www.kryptowire.com/ (report 'Kryptowire Discovers Mobile Phone Firmware that Transmitted Personally Identifiable Information', Nov 2016)

packages.name: Adups FOTA system operator
packages.purpose: Privileged helper of Adups FOTA that installs updates.
packages.evidence: Named alongside com.adups.fota in the Kryptowire 2016 report as one of the two system apps involved.
packages.risk: Same as com.adups.fota: OTA updates stop while it is disabled.

packages.name: Redstone FOTA (firmware updater)
packages.purpose: Over-the-air firmware updates from the OTA supplier Redstone.
packages.evidence: Malwarebytes (Apr 2021) detects it as Android/PUP.Riskware.Autoins.Redstone after a compromised update environment pushed a trojan downloader to Gigaset phones through it. Redstone and Gigaset say the app itself contains no malware.
packages.risk: It is the firmware updater: OTA updates stop while it is disabled.

packages.name: TWCore (DoFun head units)
packages.purpose: DoFun's system app that collects device telemetry and pushes OTA system updates.
packages.evidence: Kaspersky (2026) found TWCore downloading and installing APKs from a server; in every observed infection the malicious JarService (com.tw.jar1) was installed by com.tw.core. The vendor reported the issue fixed.
packages.risk: It is the unit's updater and may do more on DoFun firmware. Disabling it stops OTA updates; test vehicle functions afterwards. Blocking its network (Privacy Shield app block) is the gentler option.

packages.name: JarService
packages.purpose: No legitimate purpose known. Headless app with no launcher icon.
packages.evidence: Kaspersky (2026) identifies com.tw.jar1 'JarService' as the multi-stage downloader installed through TWCore, used for ad fraud and residential-proxy botnet enrolment.
packages.risk: Disabling it is not a clean-up: a unit that has it should be considered compromised. Ask the seller for fixed firmware.

packages.name: Google Feedback
packages.purpose: Sends a report when you choose 'Send feedback' or an app crash report is submitted.
packages.evidence: Google's feedback client. Reports are user-initiated; CleanYourTV lists it for the same reason.
packages.risk: Crash and feedback dialogs stop offering to send a report. Nothing else is known to depend on it.

domains.note: Received the personal data collected by old Adups FOTA versions.
Could issue remote commands to Adups FOTA.

domains.source: Reported as the MQTT broker of the DoFun campaign in write-ups of Kaspersky's 2026 report; not confirmed here against the original IOC list.
domains.note: Check the Kaspersky report before relying on it.
